newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa's heart worries doctors.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa's heart worries doctors.

text.p: Mother Teresa suffered more chest pain early on Tuesday and the Roman Catholic missionary's doctor said he was worried about her nagging heart problems.

"Her heart failure and irregular heart beats are still persisting and we are worried," Dr A.K. Bardhan, Mother Teresa's personal cardiologist, told Reuters at Woodlands Nursing Home in the eastern Indian city of Calcutta.
Known as the "Saint of the Gutters" for her work with the world's downtrodden, the 86-year-old nun was admitted to hospital with an irregular heart beat early on Friday.
She has suffered heart failure three times since last Thursday.
Bardhan said the doctors wanted to do surgery but the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner was balking.

"We have to do some invasive cardiology. But she is reluctant," he said. "She may just say no. She is a very stubborn lady." Mother Teresa was fitted with a heart pacemaker in 1989 and underwent heart surgery in 1991 in the United States and again in 1993 in Calcutta, India's most densely populated city, which she has made her home.
Doctors were considering performing angioplasty, in which surgeons insert a balloon into blood vessels to clear them of obstructions. She underwent the same procedure in 1993.
Bardhan said Mother Teresa, who remains in intensive cardiac care, suffered more chest pain and lung congestion early on Tuesday.
"She is sleeping now after having mild chest pain early this morning," he said. "Her condition remains unchanged."
"Her rate of progress is very slow," Dr S.K. Sen, the hospital's medical director, said. "She has chest pain and heart failure because of lung congestion."
Since being fitted with the heart pacemaker, Mother Teresa has spent time in hospital for heart disease, bacterial pneumonia, broken ribs malaria and lung problems.
When she was rushed to Woodlands Nursing Home last week, it was the third time since last August that she had been admitted for emergency care.
She had heart failure in August, then fell and hit her head in September.
But each time she returned to her Missionaries of Charity religious order, which cares for the poor and destitute in dozens of countries.
Earlier this month Mother Teresa received honorary American citizenship, one of only five people in U.S. history, in a ceremony led by U.S. Ambassador to India Frank Wisner.
She began her life's work in the slums of Calcutta in 1949 and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.
